paragraphs.context: For several years I’ve wanted Jack and Annie to visit Native American people in the 1800s.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The writer wanted Jack and Annie to visit Native Americans.
paragraphs.simple: For years the writer wanted to send Jack and Annie to visit Native American people in the 1800s. But there are many different tribes, and each one has its own customs, language and way of life, so it was hard to choose.
paragraphs.tone: Careful and respectful. The writer wants to be fair to real people.

background.note: Native Americans are the first peoples of North America. There were hundreds of different nations (tribes), each with its own language and customs.

paragraphs.context: Finally, I settled on the Lakota, a tribe of the Great Plains.
paragraphs.simple: She chose the Lakota, a tribe of the Great Plains. Research was hard, because there were several Lakota groups, and many of their customs were never written down.

background.note: The Lakota are one of the Sioux peoples. In the 1800s they lived on the northern Great Plains and followed the buffalo herds.
The Great Plains is a huge, flat area of grassland in the middle of North America, from Canada down to Texas.

paragraphs.context: But in Buffalo Before Breakfast, I have tried to share with you the most basic information
paragraphs.mainIdea: She shares the basic facts she learned.
paragraphs.simple: In this book she tells you the most important things she learned about the old Lakota ways. She, Jack and Annie feel lucky to "visit" these people, and she hopes you will too.

paragraphs.context: In Magic Tree House Books #17–20, Jack and Annie must be given four special gifts
paragraphs.mainIdea: The story so far: the gifts for Teddy.
paragraphs.simple: In books 17 to 20, Jack and Annie must be given four gifts to free a magic dog from a spell. They got the first gift on the Titanic. Now they are going to look for the second gift.

background.note: In book #17, Tonight on the Titanic, Jack and Annie got a silver pocket watch from Lucy on the sinking ship Titanic.

paragraphs.context: A small dog stood in the early sunlight.
paragraphs.simple: Jack sees a little dog outside in the morning sun. It has soft hanging ears and messy brown hair. It is Teddy!

paragraphs.context: “Breakfast will be ready soon,” she said.
paragraphs.simple: Mom says breakfast is almost ready, and Grandmother will come very soon. Jack loves her visits.
paragraphs.tone: This is a clue for the book title: they must be back before breakfast.

paragraphs.context: They ran between the trees. Wind rattled the leaves.
paragraphs.simple: The wind shakes the leaves noisily. Birds fly quickly down from branch to branch.

paragraphs.context: Inside the tree house, Teddy sniffed a silver pocket watch on the floor.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The watch from the Titanic is still there.
paragraphs.simple: Teddy smells the silver watch. Next to it is Morgan's note.

paragraphs.context: The time on the watch was 2:20—the time the Titanic had sunk.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The watch reminds them of the Titanic.
paragraphs.simple: The watch still shows 2:20, the time the Titanic went down. They remember that sad night.

paragraphs.context: He picked up a book in the corner.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book for this trip: The Great Plains.
paragraphs.simple: Jack finds a book with a picture of a wide, grassy land. It is called The Great Plains.

paragraphs.context: “Let’s go,” said Annie. “The sooner we free Teddy, the better.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie wants to free Teddy quickly.
paragraphs.simple: Annie means: if we free Teddy soon, that is good. "The sooner, the better" means as soon as possible.

paragraphs.context: Their jeans and T-shirts had magically changed.
paragraphs.simple: Magic has changed their clothes. Jack has a shirt and pants made of soft deer leather. Annie has a leather dress with strings hanging along the edges.

background.note: Buckskin is soft leather made from deer skin. Plains peoples and early American hunters wore buckskin clothes.

paragraphs.context: They both wore soft leather boots and coonskin caps.
paragraphs.simple: They both wear soft leather boots and caps made of raccoon fur. Jack's backpack is now a leather bag.

background.note: A coonskin cap is made from raccoon fur, with the tail hanging down at the back. It was worn by American frontiersmen like Davy Crockett.

paragraphs.context: “I feel like a mountain man,” he said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack feels like a mountain man.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks he looks like an old American hunter of the mountains. Annie jokes: you only need a mountain.

background.note: Mountain men were American and Canadian hunters and fur traders in the Rocky Mountains in the early 1800s.

paragraphs.context: The tree house sat in a lone tree in a vast golden prairie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house is in a huge grassland.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house is in the only tree on a huge, golden prairie. The sun is coming up far away.

paragraphs.context: Wind whispered through the tall yellow grass.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The wind in the grass sounds like a whisper.
paragraphs.simple: The wind moves through the tall grass with a soft sound: shh, shh, shh.
paragraphs.tone: The writer makes the wind sound like a person whispering. This is a quiet, peaceful picture.

paragraphs.context: The Great Plains are in the middle of the United States.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Facts from the book: the Great Plains.
paragraphs.simple: The Great Plains are in the middle of the U.S. Before 1900 this huge grassland covered almost one fifth of the country. People called it "an ocean of grass".

background.note: The 20th century means the years 1901 to 2000. So "before the 20th century" means before about 1900.

paragraphs.context: When he stepped onto the ground, the grass came all the way up to his chest.
paragraphs.simple: The grass is as high as Jack's chest. It touches his nose and makes him sneeze.

paragraphs.context: The wind blew gently as Jack hurried after her.
paragraphs.simple: Jack can only see grass moving up and down in the wind, like waves on the sea.

paragraphs.context: But he kept going through the tall, rippling grass.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack sees something at the top of the hill.
paragraphs.simple: They walk down a small slope and up a small hill. At the top, Jack suddenly stops and does not move.
paragraphs.tone: The chapter ends before we see what Jack sees. We want to read on.

paragraphs.context: Jack stared at a circle of tepees ahead.
paragraphs.simple: Jack sees a circle of tepees. People in leather clothes are busy. Horses eat grass nearby.

background.note: A tepee is a cone-shaped tent made of buffalo skins on long poles. It could be taken down quickly when the people moved to follow the buffalo. The door usually faced east, toward the sunrise.

paragraphs.context: In the early 1800s, many different Native American tribes lived on the Great Plains.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Facts from the book: the Lakota.
paragraphs.simple: In the early 1800s, many tribes lived on the Great Plains. The Lakota were the largest. They lived mostly in what is now North Dakota, South Dakota and Minnesota.

paragraphs.context: The sun was very bright behind the rider.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A rider with a bow comes near.
paragraphs.simple: The sun is behind the rider, so Jack can only see his shape. He has a bow and a bag of arrows on his back.

paragraphs.context: Everything changed for the Native Americans of the Great Plains after white settlers arrived in the mid-1800s.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Facts from the book: the settlers came.
paragraphs.simple: After white settlers came in the middle of the 1800s, there was fighting. By 1900 the Lakota had lost the war. They lost their land and their old way of life.

background.note: In the mid-1800s, many white Americans moved west to farm and look for gold. They took land where Native Americans lived, and the U.S. Army fought the tribes.
In 1890 the U.S. Army killed many Lakota at Wounded Knee, in South Dakota. This is often seen as the end of the Plains wars.

paragraphs.context: “This might be a time when the Indians are fighting with the settlers,” said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is afraid there may be fighting.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks they may have come at a time of war, so it could be dangerous.

background.note: Columbus thought he had reached India, so Europeans called the people of America "Indians". Today many people say "Native Americans" or use the name of each nation, like "Lakota".

paragraphs.context: “Wait!” shouted Jack. He jumped up from the grass. “We come in peace!”
paragraphs.simple: Jack jumps up and says they have not come to fight.

paragraphs.context: Now Jack saw that he was only a boy on a pony.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The rider is only a boy.
paragraphs.simple: The "warrior" is just a boy of ten or eleven on a small horse.

paragraphs.context: “Black Hawk,” he said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The boy's name is Black Hawk.
paragraphs.simple: The boy says his name is Black Hawk. A hawk is a strong bird that hunts.

background.note: Lakota names often came from animals, nature or something brave a person did. Names could change during a person's life.

paragraphs.context: What if the Lakota are at war with the white settlers?
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks: maybe the Lakota are fighting the settlers. Maybe they will think we are enemies.

paragraphs.context: Good manners to the Lakota mean speaking as few words as possible and sharing gifts when visiting.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Facts from the book: Lakota manners.
paragraphs.simple: For the Lakota, being polite means not talking too much and giving gifts when you visit someone.

paragraphs.context: Holding up two fingers means “friend.”
paragraphs.simple: If you hold up two fingers, it means "friend".

background.note: Plains peoples spoke many different languages, so they used a hand-sign language to talk with each other. The sign for "friend" shows two fingers held up together.

paragraphs.context: Ahead of them, the people at the campsite had stopped what they were doing.
paragraphs.simple: All the people in the camp stop working and look at Jack and Annie.

paragraphs.context: He glanced at Annie. She walked tall and straight.
paragraphs.simple: Annie walks with her back straight and her chin up. Her face is calm. Jack does the same and feels braver.

paragraphs.context: Inside, the tepee looked like a small round room.
paragraphs.simple: The tepee is like a small round room. A fire burns in the middle, and the smoke goes out of a hole at the top.

paragraphs.context: An old woman sat on animal skins.
paragraphs.simple: An old woman sits on animal skins. She is sewing small colored balls onto a soft leather shoe.

background.note: Moccasins are soft leather shoes. Lakota women decorated them with beads or colored porcupine quills.

paragraphs.context: Then Jack took off his coonskin cap. He gave it to Grandmother.
paragraphs.simple: Jack remembers the good manners: he gives Grandmother his fur cap as a gift. She puts it on and laughs.

paragraphs.context: Men and boys carved bows.
paragraphs.simple: Men and boys make bows from wood. Women and girls beat meat to make it soft and sew clothes. A girl puts bear claws on a shirt.

background.note: Lakota women dried buffalo meat and pounded it with berries and fat to make "pemmican", a food that could be kept for months.

paragraphs.context: “The bear claws will give her the strength of the bear,” said Grandmother.
paragraphs.simple: Grandmother says the bear claws give the girl a bear's strength. Feathers, teeth and quills give her the power of other animals too.

background.note: Before glass beads came from Europe, Plains women colored porcupine quills and sewed them onto clothes in beautiful patterns.
Feathers from hawks and eagles were special to the Lakota because these birds fly high, close to the sky.

paragraphs.context: “The buffalo gives our people many gifts,” said the old woman.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The buffalo gives the Lakota everything.
paragraphs.simple: The Lakota use every part of the buffalo: meat for food, skin for tepees, bones for tools, horns for cups, hair for ropes and ribs for sleds.

background.note: The buffalo was the center of Plains life. People used it for food, clothes, homes, tools, glue and even fuel (dried buffalo dung for fires).

paragraphs.context: “That reminds me of the seal hunter in the Arctic,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie remembers a hunter in the Arctic who used every part of a seal and did not waste anything.

background.note: In Magic Tree House #12, Polar Bears Past Bedtime, Jack and Annie met a seal hunter in the Arctic.

paragraphs.context: The fierce wolf was Black Hawk wearing a wolf’s hide!
paragraphs.simple: It is not a real wolf. It is Black Hawk in a wolf skin. His head comes out through a cut near the wolf's neck.

background.note: Plains hunters sometimes wore wolf skins to creep close to buffalo. Buffalo were not afraid of a single wolf, so they did not run away.

paragraphs.context: “Lakota never take more buffalo than we need,” she said.
paragraphs.simple: Grandmother says the Lakota only hunt the buffalo they need. They do not waste.

paragraphs.context: “Annie,” whispered Jack. “How are we going to ride without saddles or reins?”
paragraphs.simple: Jack is worried: there is no seat and no straps to control the ponies. Annie says to hold the horse's hair and hold on with your legs.

background.note: Plains peoples were famous riders. Children learned to ride very young, often with no saddle at all.

paragraphs.context: Annie threw her arms around Midnight’s neck.
paragraphs.simple: Annie holds the pony's neck, swings her leg over its back and pulls herself up.

paragraphs.context: He liked Grandmother. He wanted her to admire him.
paragraphs.simple: Jack wants Grandmother to think he is brave. He shouts loudly, and his pony runs very fast.

paragraphs.context: Shadows of clouds swept over the plains.
paragraphs.simple: The shadows of clouds move quickly over the grass. They look like big dark birds with open wings.
paragraphs.tone: A beautiful picture. The writer compares the shadows to birds.

paragraphs.context: Before them were thousands and thousands of grazing buffalo.
paragraphs.simple: In front of them there are thousands of buffalo eating grass.

paragraphs.context: The true name of the buffalo is “bison.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Facts from the book: how many buffalo.
paragraphs.simple: In 1800 there were about 40 million bison on the Great Plains. 100 years later there were fewer than 300. White hunters and soldiers killed almost all of them.

background.note: Hunters killed bison for their skins and sometimes just for sport. Trains carried shooters across the plains. Today there are again about 500,000 bison in North America, mostly on farms.

paragraphs.context: Now Jack knew for certain they’d come to the time before the white settlers
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack knows what time they are in.
paragraphs.simple: Because there are so many buffalo, Jack is sure they are in the time before the settlers and soldiers came.

paragraphs.context: He began creeping on all fours toward the buffalo.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Black Hawk creeps toward the buffalo.
paragraphs.simple: Black Hawk moves slowly on his hands and knees toward the herd.

paragraphs.context: A bison can weigh two thousand pounds and stand six feet high.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Facts from the book: bison are big and dangerous.
paragraphs.simple: A bison can be about 900 kg and almost 2 meters tall. If one gets afraid, it may run and make the whole herd run wildly.

background.note: 2,000 pounds is about 900 kg; six feet is about 1.8 meters. A bison can run at about 55 km an hour.

paragraphs.context: Black Hawk stopped just as he was passing the nearest buffalo.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Black Hawk is going to sneeze.
paragraphs.simple: Black Hawk's eyes close tight, his nose makes lines, and his mouth opens. He is going to sneeze!
paragraphs.tone: Funny and scary at the same time. Jack sneezed earlier too.

paragraphs.context: The huge buffalo jerked its head up.
paragraphs.simple: The buffalo lifts its head fast, makes a low sound, points its horns and runs at Black Hawk.

paragraphs.context: The dog tore down the hill.
paragraphs.simple: Teddy runs down the hill very fast and jumps along the side of the herd, barking loudly.

paragraphs.context: Sunlight slowed as Black Hawk got near.
paragraphs.simple: Jack's pony slows down. Black Hawk jumps onto its back. The pony turns away from the buffalo and runs up the hill.

paragraphs.context: Annie was surrounded by buffalo—calm buffalo.
paragraphs.simple: Buffalo are all around Annie, but they are calm. She is touching and talking to them. Slowly the whole herd stops running.

paragraphs.context: “She has good medicine,” said Black Hawk.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Black Hawk says Annie has special power.
paragraphs.simple: Black Hawk means Annie has power from the spirits. Jack thinks he means medicine from a doctor.

background.note: For the Lakota and other Plains peoples, "medicine" also meant spiritual power: a special power or help from the spirit world.

paragraphs.context: “I was trying to find Teddy,” said Annie,
paragraphs.simple: Annie got in front of the running buffalo. She held up her hands and shouted "Stop!" Then a beautiful woman in white came to help her.

paragraphs.context: “You saw the spirit of White Buffalo Woman,” he said.
paragraphs.simple: Black Hawk says the lady was White Buffalo Woman, a holy spirit.

background.note: White Buffalo Woman is a holy figure in Lakota belief. The story says she brought the sacred pipe to the Lakota and taught them how to pray. (See the legend at the end of the book.)

paragraphs.context: The sun was going down as the three ponies galloped for home.
paragraphs.simple: The sun is setting. The sky has lines of gold and red light. The tepees shine in the evening sun.

paragraphs.context: “Let this be a lesson to you,” Grandmother said sternly.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Grandmother teaches Black Hawk a lesson.
paragraphs.simple: Grandmother says: you were too proud, so you showed off. That made you act in a silly way. You frightened one buffalo, and it frightened the others. One thing causes the next. Everything is connected.
paragraphs.tone: Serious, but kind. This is the big idea of the book.

paragraphs.context: “Buffalo Girl and Rides-Like-Wind showed great courage today,” she said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack and Annie get Lakota names.
paragraphs.simple: Grandmother gives them new names: Annie is "Buffalo Girl" and Jack is "Rides-Like-Wind". Jack loves his name.

paragraphs.context: The evening shadows spread over the camp.
paragraphs.simple: It is getting dark. Someone plays a drum. It sounds like a heart beating.

background.note: For many Native American peoples, the drum is like the heartbeat of the earth.

paragraphs.context: An old man held a long pipe up to the sky.
paragraphs.simple: An old man holds up a long pipe and points it to the east, south, west and north. Then he gives it to the next man.

background.note: The pipe ceremony is very sacred for the Lakota. The smoke carries prayers up to the Great Spirit. Pointing to the four directions honors all parts of the world.

paragraphs.context: “The smoke from the sacred pipe joins all things to the Great Spirit,”
paragraphs.simple: Grandmother says the smoke joins everything to the Great Spirit.

background.note: "Wakan Tanka" in Lakota, often translated as "the Great Spirit" or "the Great Mystery": the holy power in all things.

paragraphs.context: “The Great Spirit is the source of all things in the sacred circle of life,” said Grandmother.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Everything comes from the Great Spirit.
paragraphs.simple: All things come from the Great Spirit. All the spirits come from it too.

background.note: The circle is very important in Lakota belief: the sun, the moon, the seasons and life itself go around in circles. Tepees and camps were round too.

paragraphs.context: “She is a messenger of the Great Spirit,” said Grandmother.
paragraphs.simple: The Great Spirit sent White Buffalo Woman when the people were very hungry. She brought the sacred pipe so their prayers could go up. The Great Spirit answers by sending buffalo.

paragraphs.context: “Sometimes courage can summon help from the beyond,” Grandmother said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Courage can call help from the spirit world.
paragraphs.simple: Grandmother says that when you are brave, help can come from the world of the spirits.

paragraphs.context: “This is a gift for you,” she said. “An eagle’s feather for your courage.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: The second gift: an eagle feather.
paragraphs.simple: Grandmother gives them an eagle feather because they were brave. It is the "gift from the prairie blue".

background.note: For the Lakota, an eagle feather is a very great honor. It was given for courage. The eagle flies highest, so it is closest to the Great Spirit.

paragraphs.context: “All things are related,” he said.
paragraphs.simple: The old man says that all things in the world are connected, like one family.

background.note: This is a famous Lakota prayer: "Mitakuye Oyasin", often translated as "All my relatives" or "We are all related". It means people, animals, plants and the earth are one family.

paragraphs.context: Grandmother pointed to two buffalo robes that lay to one side of the still-burning fire.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie lie down on buffalo skins near the fire. Teddy lies between them.

paragraphs.context: It’s the voice of the Great Plains, he thought.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks the wind is the voice of the Great Plains. Then he slowly falls asleep.

paragraphs.context: In the cool light before dawn, everyone was taking down their tepees.
paragraphs.simple: Early in the morning, everyone takes down their tepees. They put them on flat frames tied to two poles, and horses pull them.

background.term: wooden platforms strapped to two poles
background.note: This is called a "travois": two long poles tied to a horse, with a frame between them. The ends drag on the ground. Plains peoples used it to move their homes.

paragraphs.context: “It is time to follow the buffalo,” said Grandmother.
paragraphs.simple: The Lakota move to a new place to follow the buffalo herds.

background.note: Plains peoples like the Lakota were nomads: they moved camp many times a year to follow the buffalo.

paragraphs.context: “People cannot own land,” he said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The land belongs to the Great Spirit.
paragraphs.simple: Black Hawk laughs. For him, people cannot have land as their own. The land belongs to the Great Spirit.

background.note: This was a big difference between Native Americans and white settlers. Settlers bought and sold land and built fences; many tribes believed land was for everyone to share.

paragraphs.context: “There is not only one place to learn,” he said.
paragraphs.simple: Black Hawk says you can learn anywhere: in camp you learn to make things, on the plains you learn to ride and hunt, and from the eagle you learn courage.

paragraphs.context: “Let your thoughts rise as high as that feather,” said Grandmother.
paragraphs.simple: Grandmother says: let your thoughts go up high, like the eagle feather. The feather has good medicine: it connects you to the spirit world.

paragraphs.context: “Soon everything will change,” he said sadly.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is sad about the future.
paragraphs.simple: Jack knows that soon the buffalo and the Lakota's old way of life will disappear. Annie says the Great Spirit will still look after them.

paragraphs.context: Bright sunlight flooded the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: Lots of sunlight fills the tree house. Their clothes are normal again.

paragraphs.context: “One second Teddy disappeared in the grass. Then White Buffalo Woman appeared,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie notices: when Teddy disappeared, White Buffalo Woman appeared, and when she disappeared, Teddy came back. Maybe Teddy is magic.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, man, as soon as we turned our backs, he slipped away,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: When they turned around, Teddy quietly left, just like last time.

paragraphs.context: Black Hawk’s grandmother is right, he thought. All things are related.
paragraphs.simple: Jack watches the wind, the trees and the birds and thinks: everything is connected.
paragraphs.tone: A peaceful ending. Jack now understands Grandmother's words.

paragraphs.context: Together they ran out of the Frog Creek woods
paragraphs.simple: They run home and into their own grandmother's arms.
paragraphs.tone: A warm ending. It matches Black Hawk's grandmother.

paragraphs.context: Long ago, when the Lakota had no game to hunt, a beautiful woman in white buckskins appeared.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The legend: White Buffalo Woman brings the pipe.
paragraphs.simple: Long ago the Lakota had no animals to hunt. A beautiful woman in white came. She gave the chief a special pipe with a buffalo carved on the bowl and eagle feathers on the stem.

paragraphs.context: The pipe bowl represented the earth.
paragraphs.simple: Each part of the pipe is a sign: the bowl is the earth, the buffalo is all four-legged animals, the stem is all growing things, and the feathers are all birds.

paragraphs.context: As White Buffalo Woman walked away from the tribe, she turned into a white buffalo calf
paragraphs.mainIdea: She becomes a white buffalo calf.
paragraphs.simple: When she left, she changed into a white baby buffalo, one of the rarest animals.

background.note: A white buffalo is extremely rare, maybe one in millions. For the Lakota, the birth of a white buffalo calf is a very holy sign.

paragraphs.context: 1) The Lakota tribe has also been called the Sioux.
paragraphs.simple: The Lakota are also called the Sioux.

background.note: "Sioux" (said "soo") is a name given by other people. The Sioux include three main groups: Lakota, Dakota and Nakota. Famous Lakota leaders include Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse.

paragraphs.context: 2) Today most Lakota live on reservations in North and South Dakota.
paragraphs.simple: Today most Lakota live on land kept for them by the U.S. government. Parents and grandparents still teach their children the old beliefs.

background.note: Pine Ridge and Rosebud in South Dakota and Standing Rock in North and South Dakota are large Lakota reservations.

paragraphs.context: 3) The true name of the buffalo is bison.
paragraphs.simple: Bison came to North America during the Ice Age. Once they were the biggest group of large animals on the continent.

paragraphs.context: 4) In the 1800s, the U.S. Army was at war with the Native Americans of the plains.
paragraphs.simple: The army knew the Native Americans could not live their old way without bison. So they decided to kill the herds. Millions were killed, and only a few hundred were left.

paragraphs.context: 5) In the early 1900s, many people were upset by the killing of the bison.
paragraphs.simple: In the early 1900s, people asked the government to save the bison. Some were sent to Yellowstone National Park and kept safe. Almost 2,500 live there today.

background.note: Yellowstone, opened in 1872, was the first national park in the world. Its bison herd is the only one in the U.S. that has lived in the same place since prehistoric times.

sentences.main: I wasn't sure which tribe they should visit.

sentences.context: Your pride led you to show off. Showing off made you behave foolishly.

sentences.grammar: "Lead someone to do" = make someone do. "Make someone + verb" (no "to"): "made you behave". "Showing off" is an -ing noun used as the subject.
